profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This facility is attributed to Prime, most likely Prime Data Centers given the California and Texas registry locations. Prime Data Centers own site states the company was established in 2017 in California and is now headquartered at 400 North Ervay Street, Dallas, Texas, under founder and CEO Nicholas Laag, and describes itself as majority founder owned. The company reports 28 data centers across 13 campuses globally with a 4 plus gigawatt expansion pipeline, and lists Silicon Valley and Dallas among its confirmed North America markets, alongside Austin, Chicago, Los Angeles, Phoenix, and Sacramento, matching both states where this registry lists a Prime facility. No building specific address, opening date, or individual MW figures for this particular registry row were located in available sourcing this session.

reading.body:
The Prime Santa Clara campus publishes 57 MW of IT capacity across 540,000 square feet of technical space. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 57 MW supports roughly 1,425 racks; at 10 kW per rack, a more conservative colocation assumption, the same load supports roughly 5,700 racks. The arithmetic is 57,000 kW divided by the assumed rack draw. Which end of that range applies depends on how the space is configured, and Prime does not publish that figure.

The three certifications qualify the campus for specific workload categories. SOC 2 Type 2 means an auditor has verified the operator's controls over security, availability, and related trust principles over a period of time, not just at a point in time. PCI DSS qualifies the facility to process or store payment card data under the card-brand compliance framework. ISO 27001 means an accredited body has certified the information security management system against that international standard. None of these certifications are AI-specific, but regulated enterprises running AI on sensitive or financial data will treat them as a baseline requirement.

Within California, this site holds the third-highest published IT capacity among the ten facilities on this site that publish a megawatt figure at all. Those ten facilities account for 356 MW of published capacity in the state, and this campus's 57 MW represents roughly 16 percent of that total. California has 103 facilities mapped in OpenStreetMap, meaning the vast majority publish no capacity figure, so the state ranking reflects only what operators have chosen to disclose, not a complete picture of installed capacity. Santa Clara County is the geographic center of the silicon supply chain, which makes this campus's power figure consequential, but the grid headroom available at this specific site is not published.
